comparison: Both strongly support the main contribution claims (C7, C8, C52, C53). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative validation through multiple benchmark simulations and computational efficiency. Peer reviewers affirm the model 'outperforms Hill-type models' and 'accurately predicts in situ force' from multiple datasets. High agreement on model value and performance.

Perfect claim overlap (C85, C86, C89, C90) regarding extreme stretch experiments. Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval notes the linear titin model matches data up to 3.38 optimal length while Hill model fails. Peer reviewer explicitly confirms accurate prediction of 'rabbit psoas myofibrils (Leonard et al. 2010)' and acknowledges titin's role in long-range stretches.

Perfect claim overlap (C96, C97) on damping assumptions. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the assumption is reasonable but speculative and requires experimental validation. Peer reviewers also express UNCERTAINTY, with concerns about mechanistic interpretation and what drives stiffness shifts in different perturbation ranges.

Perfect claim overlap (C98, C99) on potential conflict with recent experimental observations. Both evaluations rate as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes the authors appropriately await replication before model revision. Peer reviewers don't directly comment but express broader uncertainty about parameter optimization needs for different experimental findings.

Perfect claim overlap (C6, C22, C23) on the gap in existing models. Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval notes the gap motivates VEXAT development and is supported by systematic analysis. Peer reviewers affirm 'alternative models are needed' due to Hill-type limitations and confirm the value of 'a single model which can predict muscle force under all these physiologically relevant conditions.'

High claim overlap (C82, C83, C84) on divergent behavior during stretch-hold experiments. Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval emphasizes the VEXAT model's continued force development via titin versus Hill model's negative stiffness. Peer reviewers affirm the model 'outperforms Hill-type models' and 'clearly demonstrate the weaknesses of Hill models.'

Substantial claim overlap (C94, C95) on force-velocity and force-length calibration. Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval details the mathematical basis and calibration approach. Peer reviewers confirm the model 'accurately predicts in situ force' including force-length and force-velocity relations, treating differences as model characteristics rather than failures.

Partial claim overlap (C78, C79) on high-frequency perturbation performance. Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval notes quantitative VAF values compared to Kirsch et al. 1994 benchmarks. Peer reviewers confirm the model 'accurately predicts in situ force of cat soleus (Kirsch et al. 1994)' including high-frequency perturbation experiments.

Partial claim overlap (C10, C11) on acknowledged model limitations. Both evaluations support these as honest assessments. OpenEval cites phase deviations at low frequencies and failure to capture passive force enhancement. Peer reviewers note 'the combination of phenomenological and mechanistic aspects...may sometimes make it challenging to interpret' and acknowledge unresolved mechanistic questions.

Partial claim overlap (C24-C27) on limitations of existing model classes. Both evaluations support these characterizations. OpenEval notes these are well-established properties based on mathematical structure. Peer reviewers don't challenge these claims, with one confirming 'It is well established that Hill-type models do not have any mechanism by which they can predict the effect of active muscle stretch.'

Substantial claim overlap (C111, C114-C118) on why existing models cannot replicate Kirsch experiments. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on systematic analysis of model structures. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 challenging the limited comparison: 'Many other models...have incorporated mechanistic elements which allow for the prediction of force responses to muscle stretch' and questioning whether VEXAT would outperform them. Significant disagreement on adequacy of comparative analysis.

Minimal claim overlap (C108) on missing submaximal contraction phenomena. Both evaluations support this as an acknowledged limitation. OpenEval identifies this as appropriate scope limitation. Peer reviewers note uncertainty about model practicality 'for different muscles or preparations,' encompassing these unmodeled phenomena as known limitations rather than fundamental flaws.

Partial claim overlap (C67, C68) on titin-actin interaction and damping model justification. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting justified modeling choices based on experimental evidence. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, expressing concerns about assumptions and their implications, questioning mechanistic interpretation and physiological basis of model components.

Partial claim overlap (C62, C63) on modeling simplifications. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting clear justification and appropriate trade-offs for computational efficiency. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, with concerns that 'Several ad hoc modifications were described' and uncertainty about whether assumptions capture underlying physiology correctly.

Minimal claim overlap (C100) on key modeling assumption about crossbridge-titin interaction. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting transparent statement with mathematical support while acknowledging it requires experimental validation. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, expressing concerns about 'the combination of phenomenological and mechanistic aspects' limiting insight and questioning physiological basis.

Partial claim overlap (C103, C104) on titin preload assumption. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting honest presentation of modeling choice with uncertain biological validity. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, with broader concerns about mechanistic interpretation and whether model components capture underlying physiology.

Partial claim overlap (C77, C80) on VAF values and low-frequency phase limitations. OpenEval supports these claims with quantitative data from Figure 6. Peer reviewers also support, acknowledging limitations without dispute and noting challenges in interpreting model output, particularly regarding stiffness shifts across perturbation ranges.

Minimal claim overlap (C109, C110) on inferences about existing models' inability to replicate experiments. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on logical inference from structural limitations. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, directly challenging the limited comparison and questioning whether predictions about other models' performance are adequately demonstrated.

Minimal claim overlap (C9) on reproducing classical muscle properties. Both evaluations support this claim. OpenEval emphasizes simulation of multiple benchmark experiments. Peer reviewers confirm accurate prediction of force-length and force-velocity relations, treating model characteristics as demonstrated rather than failures.

Minimal claim overlap (C30, C31) on systematic analysis of why existing models fail. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on mathematical structure and Kirsch et al. 1994's explicit demonstration. Peer reviewers support the characterization of existing model limitations without challenge, providing context for model development.

Minimal claim overlap (C48) on contradictions with experimental data in recent Hill model modifications. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting valid critiques of Sartori et al. 2015 based on comparison with experimental data. Peer reviewers affirm this finding, stating results 'clearly demonstrate the weaknesses of Hill models.'
